title: Reading Ignatius and Polycarp

objectives.can: Read Ignatius's compressed, abrupt style and Polycarp's plainer one, with their new church vocabulary.

explanation.summary: Ignatius of Antioch wrote seven short letters on his way to Rome as a prisoner, probably in the early second century (the exact date is debated). Polycarp of Smyrna wrote one letter, to the church at Philippi. Ignatius is urgent and compressed; Polycarp is plainer and borrows much of his wording from the New Testament. Both use ordinary words in newly fixed senses for the life of the church.

sections.heading: Before you read: the text is analysed by machine
body: The Greek of Ignatius and Polycarp in this library was analysed by a program and has not been checked by hand. Many words have no analysis at all, and some labels would be corrected by a Greek reader. In Ephesians 5.1, for example, the program labels ἔσχον as a third person plural, although the sentence has ἐγώ as its subject and needs 'I had'. The lesson therefore chooses examples whose analysis is reliable, and its questions are written by hand. When the program and the grammar disagree, trust the grammar.

sections.heading: Ignatius: short, urgent, packed
body: Ignatius writes as a man under arrest who is about to die (in 1.2 of Ephesians he calls himself δεδεμένον, 'bound'), and his Greek shows it. He gives commands in the third person: μηδεὶς πλανάσθω (5.2) is a present imperative, 'let no one be deceived'. He argues from the lesser to the greater with the phrase πόσῳ μᾶλλον, 'how much more'. In 5.1 he says that if he, in a short time, had such a relationship with their overseer, how much more does he count the Ephesians happy. The same phrase returns in 5.2 for the prayer of the whole church.

He also likes images and invented words. In 4.1 the presbytery is fitted to the bishop 'as strings to a harp' (ὡς χορδαὶ κιθάρᾳ). Many of his compounds, such as ἀξιονόμαστον in that verse, are rare or unique, and the program has not analysed them. Do not stop at them: the sentence usually carries on in plain Greek around the unfamiliar word.

sections.heading: Quoted and echoed Scripture
body: Ephesians 5.3 has a formal quotation: γέγραπται γάρ, 'for it is written', followed by Ὑπερηφάνοις ὁ θεὸς ἀντιτάσσεται, 'God sets himself against the proud'. The verb takes a dative of the person opposed. The same saying stands in James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5, and is usually identified as a line of the Greek book of Proverbs; the Septuagint is not yet analysed in this library, so you cannot compare the wording here. After the quotation Ignatius turns it into a call to action with an aorist subjunctive, σπουδάσωμεν, 'let us make an effort'.

Polycarp quotes less formally and echoes more. In 5.3 the list οὔτε πόρνοι οὔτε μαλακοὶ …, closing with βασιλείαν θεοῦ κληρονομήσουσιν, is close to 1 Corinthians 6:9–10. Whether Polycarp is quoting that letter directly or a common stock of teaching is a question for scholars; the wording itself shows that New Testament phrases were already familiar in the church.

sections.heading: Polycarp: plain, listing, many clauses in one sentence
body: Polycarp 5.2 is one long sentence. It gives a list of adjectives for deacons (ἄμεμπτοι, ἐγκρατεῖς, εὔσπλαγχνοι and others), then a relative clause about the Lord (ὃς ἐγένετο διάκονος πάντων), then a καθώς clause and two ἐάν clauses. The subjunctive and future that follow ἐάν are the ones you have met: the condition is open, and the main clause is a future (ἀποληψόμεθα, 'we shall receive').

Compare Ignatius. His sentences are short and each makes one demand. Polycarp stacks qualities and conditions in a single sentence, and the lists of qualities recall those of the Pastoral Letters (compare μὴ διλόγους for deacons in 1 Timothy 3:8 with μὴ δίλογοι here).

sections.heading: New church vocabulary
body: Several words in these letters are not new Greek words but ordinary words used in a fixed sense for the Christian community. The table gives the sense in the New Testament and in these authors. Scholars disagree about how fast the church's offices took the shape that Ignatius assumes, and the table does not settle that; it describes how the words are used.

Two of the words stand in the texts without a hand-checked analysis. καθολικὴ ἐκκλησία (Smyrnaeans 8.2) and Χριστιανισμός (Magnesians 10.3, Romans 3.3) are not in the New Testament and the program has not analysed them, so the questions about them are written by hand.

head: Word
In the New Testament
In Ignatius and Polycarp
rows: 'overseer': used of church officers (Acts 20:28, Philippians 1:1, 1 Timothy 3:2, Titus 1:7) and of Christ as overseer of souls (1 Peter 2:25)
One man at the head of a local church, named beside the presbytery and the deacons (Ephesians 2.2, 4.1, 5.1)
'a council of elders': the Jewish council (Acts 22:5) or a group laying on hands (1 Timothy 4:14)
The council of presbyters of a church, fitted to the bishop in Ephesians 4.1
'servant, attendant' (John 2:5, Romans 13:4) and a church office (Philippians 1:1, 1 Timothy 3:8)
A church office, but Polycarp 5.2 also calls the Lord διάκονος πάντων, 'servant of all', so the two senses meet
Ephesians 5.2: ἐντὸς τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου, 'inside the altar-place'. Polycarp 4.3 calls the widows θυσιαστήριον θεοῦ, a figure of speech
Not found in the New Testament
Smyrnaeans 8.2: ἡ καθολικὴ ἐκκλησία, the church as a whole, as against one gathering. Scholars debate whether it already means 'universal' in a fixed sense
Magnesians 10.3, Romans 3.3: the way of life and belief of those called Christians, formed as Ἰουδαϊσμός is (Galatians 1:13)

misunderstandings: μηδεὶς πλανάσθω is not a statement. A third person imperative gives a command to someone who is not being addressed directly: 'let no one be deceived'.

ἐπίσκοπος does not always mean the later 'bishop' of a diocese. In Philippians 1:1 and Acts 20:28 the word is plural, and in 1 Peter 2:25 it is applied to Christ. In Ignatius it names one man in a local church. Read each author on his own terms.
Ignatius's rare compounds are not mistakes. If the program has not analysed a word, try the parts and read on.
Polycarp's echoes of the New Testament do not prove which book he had in front of him. Shared wording shows a relationship, not its direction or the exact source.

deeper.heading: Two letters, one chapter each
body: Ignatius's letters survive in more than one form, and scholars long argued about which form is original; the library's analysed text is a single form, and this lesson does not depend on the choice. Polycarp's letter to the Philippians is unusual in mentioning his own earlier correspondence with Ignatius, which is one reason the two are read together.

quoted.title: Ignatius of Antioch, To the Ephesians
quoted.reference: Ignatius of Antioch, To the Ephesians 5.1
quoted.english: For if I in a short time gained such fellowship with your bishop as was not human but spiritual, how much more do I count you blessed who are so united with him as the Church is with Jesus Christ, and as Jesus Christ is with the Father, that all things may sound together in unison!
quoted.credit: GoLearn Greek analyser adapter-el@1 (Wiktionary Ancient Greek tables via kaikki.org); form index of the MorphGNT New Testament (James Tauber et al.); glosses from the Dodson Greek Lexicon

examples.analysis: ἐπίσκοπον is an accusative singular after πρός: 'towards your overseer'. οὖσαν is a present participle, feminine accusative, agreeing with συνήθειαν: a relationship that is 'not human but spiritual'. πόσῳ μᾶλλον, 'how much more', starts the main clause: if so short a time gave him that bond, then the Ephesians, who are joined to their overseer as the ἐκκλησία is to Jesus Christ, are all the more to be counted happy. μακαρίζω is 'I count happy'. The program has not analysed ἐγκεκραμένους or ἑνότητι, and it labels ἔσχον wrongly.

quoted.title: Ignatius of Antioch, To the Ephesians
quoted.reference: Ignatius of Antioch, To the Ephesians 5.2
quoted.english: Let no man be deceived: unless a man be within the sanctuary he lacks the bread of God, for if the prayer of one or two has such might, how much more has that of the bishop and of the whole Church?
quoted.credit: GoLearn Greek analyser adapter-el@1 (Wiktionary Ancient Greek tables via kaikki.org); form index of the MorphGNT New Testament (James Tauber et al.); glosses from the Dodson Greek Lexicon

examples.analysis: πλανάσθω is a present imperative, third person singular, passive in sense: 'let no one be deceived'. ᾖ is a present subjunctive of εἰμί in the ἐάν clause: 'if anyone is not inside …'. θυσιαστηρίου is a genitive after ἐντός: 'inside the altar'. The sentence says that such a person 'lacks the bread of God' (ἄρτου is the genitive of what is lacked). Whether Ignatius means a physical altar or the gathered community is discussed by scholars; the grammar does not decide it. Then πόσῳ μᾶλλον again, with ἔχει as the verb of the 'if' clause.

quoted.title: Ignatius of Antioch, To the Ephesians
quoted.reference: Ignatius of Antioch, To the Ephesians 5.3
quoted.english: So then he who does not join in the common assembly, is already haughty, and has separated himself. For it is written God resisteth the proud: let us then be careful not to oppose the bishop, that we may be subject to God.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Greek analyser adapter-el@1 (Wiktionary Ancient Greek tables via kaikki.org); form index of the MorphGNT New Testament (James Tauber et al.); glosses from the Dodson Greek Lexicon

examples.analysis: γέγραπται, perfect passive, introduces a quotation: 'it stands written'. In Ὑπερηφάνοις ὁ θεὸς ἀντιτάσσεται the subject is ὁ θεός and the dative ὑπερηφάνοις is the person opposed. σπουδάσωμεν is an aorist subjunctive, first person plural, urging: 'let us strive'. The infinitive after it, which is not analysed by the program, says what to strive not to do.

quoted.title: Ignatius of Antioch, To the Ephesians
quoted.reference: Ignatius of Antioch, To the Ephesians 4.1
quoted.english: Therefore it is fitting that you should live in harmony with the will of the bishop, as indeed you do. For your justly famous presbytery, worthy of God, is attuned to the bishop as the strings to a harp. Therefore by your concord and harmonious love Jesus Christ is being sung.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Greek analyser adapter-el@1 (Wiktionary Ancient Greek tables via kaikki.org); form index of the MorphGNT New Testament (James Tauber et al.); glosses from the Dodson Greek Lexicon

examples.analysis: πρεσβυτέριον is a neuter noun in the nominative, the subject: the council of elders. The picture that follows is of strings fitted to a harp (ὡς χορδαὶ κιθάρᾳ), but the program has not analysed those words or the verb συνήρμοσται that carries it. Most of this verse is not analysed by the program, which shows how much of Ignatius needs a careful reader.

quoted.title: Polycarp, Epistle to the Philippians
quoted.reference: Polycarp of Smyrna, Polycarp, Epistle to the Philippians 5.3
quoted.credit: GoLearn Greek analyser adapter-el@1 (Wiktionary Ancient Greek tables via kaikki.org); form index of the MorphGNT New Testament (James Tauber et al.); glosses from the Dodson Greek Lexicon

examples.analysis: κληρονομήσουσιν is a future indicative, third person plural, 'they will inherit', and it echoes 1 Corinthians 6:9–10. ἀπέχεσθαι is a present middle infinitive, 'to keep away from', with ἀπό. πρεσβυτέροις and διακόνοις are datives, the persons to whom the readers are to submit. Notice the plainer, listing style compared with Ignatius.
